paragraphs: A flat picture can appear to contain three-dimensional objects or spaces. This paper investigates whether depth-estimation systems make a similar mistake: interpreting depicted depth as actual physical depth. The authors find that these illusions can seriously mislead systems using a single image, stereo image pairs, or multiple views.

To study the problem systematically, they collect a dataset with almost 3,000 scenes and 200,000 images for training and evaluating depth-estimation methods. They also introduce a framework that combines depth inferred from a single image with depth derived from binocular disparity. A vision-language model supplies common-sense information to guide how the two estimates are combined adaptively.

The experiments show that leading methods across all three input settings are vulnerable to various visual illusions, while the proposed framework achieves the strongest reported performance. The contribution is both an evaluation resource and a method for handling conflicting depth cues. The findings show that access to additional views does not, by itself, prevent the tested systems from being fooled by apparent three-dimensional structure.
neurips-2025-3d-visual-illusion-depth-es.tldr: A new dataset reveals visual-illusion failures in depth estimation, and a vision-language-guided fusion method improves performance.

paragraphs: This paper asks how accurately score-based neural generative models can learn an unknown distribution from independent samples. Its starting assumption is that the distribution is sub-Gaussian, which restricts how much probability lies far into its tails. The analysis establishes approximation and estimation guarantees without several stronger assumptions used in previous work.

The authors prove that a deep ReLU network of controlled width and depth exists that approximates the required scores with mean squared error of order one over the sample count, up to logarithmic factors. The result applies over a specified range of diffusion times. The score-estimation rate also depends on dimension and the earliest included time, so the guarantee explicitly connects statistical accuracy with how close estimation proceeds toward the original distribution.

With additional Sobolev or Besov smoothness assumptions and suitable early stopping, the models attain convergence rates close to the best possible worst-case rates, apart from logarithmic factors. The analysis does not require Lipschitz-continuous scores or a strictly positive density lower bound. These are conditional theoretical guarantees that broaden the distributions covered by existing score-model theory.
neurips-2025-approximation-and-generaliz.tldr: The paper establishes score-model approximation and learning guarantees under weaker distributional assumptions, with near-optimal rates under additional smoothness.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend substantial computation producing extended reasoning even when parts of a problem are easy. This paper studies how to adjust that effort during generation. It separates the problem into two decisions: how to steer a model toward faster or slower thinking, and when each mode is useful.

The authors identify a steering vector in the model's internal representation space that controls transitions between slower and faster reasoning. Editing representations along this direction changes reasoning effort at inference time and outperforms the prompt-based scaling methods in their comparisons. They then estimate difficulty as reasoning unfolds, using that signal to assign less effort to easy segments and more effort to complex ones.

Across the evaluated reasoning models and benchmarks, the combined method produces an average accuracy improvement of 1.3% while reducing token use by 8.6%. The authors describe it as requiring no training or additional cost and implement it using vLLM. These results support adapting effort within a reasoning process, rather than assigning the same thinking intensity to every step.
neurips-2025-controlling-thinking-speed-.tldr: Internal representation steering and live difficulty estimation let reasoning models vary their effort, improving average accuracy while using fewer tokens.

paragraphs: Cross-view geo-localization finds the location of a street photograph by matching it to an aerial image. The same place can look very different from those viewpoints, and unrelated visual factors can distract the model. The proposed CLGT framework addresses both problems by combining causal feature learning with information about road structure.

Its Causal Feature Extractor uses causal intervention to encourage representations based on stable, relevant meaning while reducing the influence of confounding factors. A separate Geometric Topology Fusion module adds bird's-eye-view road topology to the street-image features. This gives the matching process structural information that helps bridge extreme perspective changes. A data-adaptive pooling module further emphasizes regions with rich semantic information.

The authors evaluate CLGT on CVUSA and CVACT, together with robustness-focused variants containing challenging corruptions. They report state-of-the-art performance, particularly under those corruptions. The results support combining stable visual semantics with road topology: one component addresses misleading associations, while the other makes the two viewpoints easier to reconcile. Together, they improve the tested system's ability to match street and aerial observations.
neurips-2025-cvgl-causal-learning-and-ge.tldr: CLGT combines causal feature learning and road topology to improve street-to-aerial image matching, especially under visual corruptions.

paragraphs: SDForger uses language models to generate synthetic time series, including signals with several variables evolving together. The central challenge is to make numerical sequences usable by an autoregressive language model while retaining their statistical properties and temporal behavior. The framework addresses this through a compact representation designed for learning from few samples with relatively little fine-tuning computation.

The process first converts single-variable or multivariable signals into tabular embeddings. Those embeddings are encoded as text and used to fine-tune the language model. During generation, the model samples new textual embeddings, which are decoded back into numerical time series. This representation provides the bridge between language generation and synthetic signal generation.

Across diverse datasets, SDForger outperforms existing generative models in many evaluated scenarios, both on similarity measures and on downstream forecasting tasks. Those findings assess whether the generated data resembles the originals and whether it is useful for prediction. The framework also supports textual conditioning, opening a route to time-series generation informed by language and to broader multimodal modeling.
neurips-2025-forging-time-series-with-la.tldr: SDForger encodes time series as compact text representations so language models can generate useful synthetic signals with lightweight fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Graph diffusion models generate molecules by progressively adjusting atoms and bonds as structural noise is removed. Existing formulations keep the number of atoms fixed during that process. This is restrictive when generation targets a molecular property that correlates with size, because achieving the target may call for a larger or smaller molecule.

The paper introduces GrIDDD by reformulating both noising and denoising to support monotonic node insertion and deletion. The resulting process can grow or shrink a chemical graph during generation. This expands the decisions made by the model: molecular size can change as the structure develops, instead of remaining fixed while only atom and bond assignments are adjusted.

For molecular property targeting, GrIDDD matches or exceeds existing graph diffusion models despite learning the more difficult size-adaptive task. It also performs competitively against specialized models when applied to molecular optimization. The findings show that allowing graph size to change can be compatible with strong generation performance, providing a practical direction for diffusion-based molecular design where size is part of the problem.
neurips-2025-graph-diffusion-that-can-in.tldr: GrIDDD lets molecular diffusion models grow or shrink graphs during generation while maintaining competitive property-targeting and optimization performance.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition breaks a multidimensional array into simpler components and supports tasks such as latent-variable parameter estimation. Alternating Least Squares, or ALS, is widely used for this difficult nonconvex problem, but its practical usefulness has outpaced global convergence theory. This paper investigates whether allowing more components than the tensor actually needs can provide such a guarantee.

For a third-order tensor with dimensions n by n by n and rank r much smaller than n, the authors prove global convergence of ALS with high probability under random initialization when the allowed decomposition rank scales as r squared. The result makes overparameterization a sufficient route to convergence in the stated setting. Earlier work cited in the abstract established a guarantee for a gradient-descent variant using substantially more components.

The analysis also provides guarantees for low-rank approximation, extending beyond exact decomposition. Its technical contribution is a set of matrix anticoncentration arguments for studying iterative algorithms with extra parameters. The significance is a theoretical explanation of how additional representational capacity can support a widely used solver, with the probability and initialization conditions retained.
neurips-2025-guarantees-for-alternating-.tldr: The paper proves that ALS globally converges with high probability from random initialization when a low-rank third-order tensor is sufficiently overparameterized.

paragraphs: Language-model recommenders can select an item by generating its representation one token at a time. Standard likelihood-based training and decoding treat these tokens uniformly, even though some do much more to distinguish one item from another. This paper studies that difference through information gain: how much a token reduces uncertainty about which item is being generated.

The authors find that most tokens provide little information gain, yet often receive high model scores and disproportionately influence training and decoding. They propose IGD to make token handling sensitive to decisiveness. During tuning, it reduces the weight of low-information tokens. During decoding, it rebalances choices to emphasize tokens that provide more information about the item's identity.

Experiments across four benchmark datasets and two language-model backbones show consistent improvements in recommendation accuracy and significant gains on ranking metrics against strong baselines. The results support distinguishing easy-to-predict tokens from tokens that actually resolve the recommendation decision. IGD applies that distinction at both learning and generation time, aligning the model's emphasis more closely with item discrimination.
neurips-2025-igd-token-decisiveness-mode.tldr: IGD improves language-model recommendations by emphasizing tokens that most reduce uncertainty about the selected item.

paragraphs: Balanced classification gives each class equal importance even when some classes have far fewer examples. Because directly optimizing its error is usually intractable, training relies on substitute objectives. This paper develops two families: Generalized Logit-Adjusted losses, which adjust prediction scores using class frequencies, and Generalized Class-Aware weighted losses, which combine class weighting with class-specific confidence margins.

The theory distinguishes optimal prediction with unrestricted flexibility from consistency within a particular hypothesis set. GLA losses are Bayes-consistent, but their hypothesis-set consistency holds only for complete, unbounded sets. GCA losses have that consistency for bounded or complete sets. Their bounds also deteriorate more slowly as the rarest class becomes rarer: inverse square-root dependence on its probability, compared with at least inverse dependence for GLA.

Experiments show that both families can substantially outperform straightforward class weighting and standard logit adjustment. GLA generally has a small advantage on common benchmarks, while GCA has a small advantage under severe imbalance. Thus, the stronger GCA guarantees do not translate into universal empirical superiority; the findings support both families, with different theoretical and observed strengths.
neurips-2025-improved-balanced-classific.tldr: Two generalized loss families improve balanced classification, with GCA offering stronger hypothesis-set guarantees and GLA often slightly better benchmark performance.

paragraphs: IntrinsiX generates material-property maps from text descriptions, producing assets that graphics applications can relight and edit. Ordinary generated images already contain a particular scene's lighting. By predicting physically based rendering maps instead, the method supplies separate information about surface color, roughness, metallic properties, and normals that a renderer can use under different lighting.

The system starts with separately pretrained models for each material component, drawing on strong image priors. A cross-intrinsic attention mechanism then connects their key and value features so the components exchange information and describe a coherent scene. A rendering loss adds constraints in image space, helping ground the individual maps and preserve fine detail in the predicted surface-reflection properties.

The authors report detailed outputs, strong generalization, and a significant advantage over decomposing generated images into intrinsic components using existing methods. They demonstrate relighting, editing, and text-conditioned room-scale PBR texture generation. The approach matters because it directly generates coordinated rendering inputs, making the text-driven outputs usable for graphics workflows that need control over materials and illumination.
neurips-2025-intrinsix-high-quality-pbr-.tldr: IntrinsiX turns text into coordinated material maps for detailed, editable, and relightable graphics assets.

paragraphs: Kinaema addresses a robot's need to remember places encountered during ongoing operation. As the robot moves, the model processes a stream of visual observations. When given a query image, it predicts where the depicted space lies relative to the robot's current position, allowing earlier observations to inform a later navigation task.

The model maintains a compact latent memory that a transformer updates recurrently. It compresses the observation stream into that internal state instead of explicitly retaining an ever-growing history of images. Consequently, it has no hard context-length constraint imposed by storing the observation history. The key question is whether this compressed state retains enough spatial information to remain useful.

The authors test that question with Mem-Nav, a downstream task designed around continuous robot operation. Their large-capacity recurrent model maintains useful scene information and navigates to goals seen before the current episode began. It is also computationally efficient, particularly compared with classical transformers attending over observation histories. These findings support recurrent memory as a way to reuse prior experience for navigation.
neurips-2025-kinaema-a-recurrent-sequenc.tldr: Kinaema compresses a robot's visual experience into recurrent memory to locate and navigate toward places seen before a task begins.

paragraphs: A prompt's grammatical structure can become an unintended clue about its subject area. This paper studies syntactic templates, defined as recurring sequences of part-of-speech tags, and asks whether models associate those templates with particular domains. The concern is that a learned association can sometimes outweigh what an instruction actually means.

Using synthetic training data, the authors show that correlations between syntax and domain can reduce performance on entity-knowledge tasks in OLMo-2 models ranging from 1B to 13B parameters. They also develop an evaluation framework for detecting the effect in already trained models. On a subset of FlanV2, they find it in both open and closed models, including OLMo-2-7B, Llama-4-Maverick, and GPT-4o.

A security case study shows that these unintended associations can also be used to bypass refusals in OLMo-2-7B Instruct and GPT-4o. The findings motivate explicitly testing syntax-domain correlations and increasing syntactic variety within each training domain. The broader lesson is that grammatical regularities can become shortcuts that interfere with semantic interpretation in the examined settings.
neurips-2025-learning-the-wrong-lessons-.tldr: Language models can learn misleading associations between grammatical patterns and subject areas that impair instruction interpretation and sometimes enable refusal bypasses.

paragraphs: MF-LLM models collective behavior as a feedback process between individuals and their population. Simply aggregating independently generated decisions misses how people respond to the surrounding group. The framework incorporates mean field theory into language-model social simulation so that population-level signals guide individual decisions, and those decisions subsequently change the signals.

This loop creates evolving trajectories of collective behavior. To improve agreement with observed human data, the authors introduce IB-Tune, a fine-tuning method inspired by the information bottleneck principle. It preserves population information that is predictive of future actions while filtering redundant history. The aim is to make the simulation's decisions depend on the parts of collective experience that matter for what happens next.

On a real-world social dataset, MF-LLM reduces KL divergence from human population distributions by 47% relative to baselines without mean-field modeling. The authors also report generalization across seven domains and four language-model backbones. These results support the framework's use for trend forecasting and intervention planning by showing improved quantitative alignment between simulated population behavior and the observed distribution.
neurips-2025-mf-llm-simulating-populatio.tldr: MF-LLM couples individual decisions with population feedback to produce social simulations that more closely match observed human behavior.

paragraphs: MUP reconstructs large scenes and synthesizes new camera and LiDAR views without depending on accurate input poses. Cameras provide rich texture but limited geometric information, while LiDAR point clouds provide sparse geometry without texture. Using either modality alone can leave pose optimization stuck in poor local solutions.

The framework combines the modalities through unified neural fields. A LiDAR field supplies continuous depth supervision for image reconstruction, extending beyond discrete supervision at measured points. Pose updates receive learning signals from both rendered point-cloud geometry and image texture. A multimodal geometric optimizer adds point-cloud geometric relationships and photometric regularization between neighboring image frames to further guide pose estimation.

MUP also uses a modality-specific coarse-to-fine training process to reduce differences between the inputs and obtain a compact reconstruction. Experiments on KITTI-360 and NuScenes show superior geometry-aware and modality-consistent reconstruction in the evaluated pose-free setting. The contribution is joint reconstruction and pose optimization: each sensor's strengths help constrain the other, while the framework supports novel-view synthesis for both modalities.
neurips-2025-multimodal-lidar-camera-nov.tldr: MUP jointly reconstructs camera and LiDAR observations, using complementary geometry and texture to improve novel-view synthesis without accurate input poses.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks build transformations into their architecture so that their responses change consistently when inputs are transformed. This paper targets projective transformations, an important and difficult class for vision. Existing approaches based on group or steerable convolutions face limitations here, motivating a construction based on differential invariants.

Using the moving frame method and a carefully chosen cross section for multidimensional functions, the authors derive a complete set of second-order fundamental differential invariants for the projective group. They analyze how the underlying components transform and simplify the resulting set. These mathematical ingredients form the basis of PDINet, which achieves full projective equivariance without approximating the group through discretization or sampling.

On projectively transformed STL-10 and Imagenette data, PDINet reports accuracy improvements of 11.39% and 5.66% over the respective standard baselines in out-of-distribution settings. These experiments support the value of explicitly incorporating projective symmetry for generalization to unfamiliar geometric transformations. The paper connects a rigorous invariant construction to a deep network architecture with demonstrated gains on the tested image-classification problems.
neurips-2025-projective-equivariant-netw.tldr: PDINet uses differential invariants to achieve full projective equivariance and improve classification under unfamiliar geometric transformations.

paragraphs: Locate-then-edit methods update specific knowledge in a language model by identifying important layers and changing their weights. A common procedure computes the desired correction at the final selected layer, then distributes that residual across several layers through least-squares updates. This paper finds that the distribution step can itself reduce editing precision.

The authors analyze the problem both theoretically and empirically. They show that residual distribution introduces weight-shift errors, and that these errors grow with distribution distance, batch size, and the length of an edit sequence. This identifies a mechanism through which a seemingly useful multi-layer update can lead to inaccurate or suboptimal changes, especially as editing accumulates.

To address the failure mode, they propose Boundary Layer Update, or BLUE, as a strategy for improving locate-then-edit methods. Sequential batch-editing experiments on three language models and two datasets report an average performance improvement of 35.59%, alongside better preservation of general capabilities. The contribution links a specific source of editing error to a corrective strategy, with evidence covering both successful updates and retention of broader model ability.
neurips-2025-rethinking-residual-distrib.tldr: BLUE improves targeted language-model editing by addressing weight-shift errors caused by distributing residual corrections across layers.

paragraphs: SEEA-R1 applies reinforcement fine-tuning to embodied agents that must reason and act over multiple steps. Such tasks often provide rewards only after a long sequence, making it difficult to identify useful intermediate decisions. Handcrafted reward functions introduce another obstacle because they can restrict adaptation to new tasks and environments.

The framework addresses these problems with two components. Tree-GRPO integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search into group relative policy optimization, turning sparse delayed feedback into denser intermediate learning signals. A Multimodal Generative Reward Model estimates rewards across tasks and scenes, supporting adaptation when ground-truth rewards are unavailable. Together, they aim to improve the agent's reasoning and behavior through reward-driven learning.

On ALFWorld, SEEA-R1 achieves reported scores of 85.07% for textual interaction and 46.27% for multimodal interaction, exceeding prior methods including GPT-4o. Without ground-truth reward, it scores 80.3% and 44.03%, respectively, surpassing all evaluated open-source baselines. These results support the framework's potential for agents that improve through interaction, with evidence for both tree-based feedback and operation using learned reward estimates.
neurips-2025-seea-r1-tree-structured-rei.tldr: SEEA-R1 combines tree-based reinforcement learning and multimodal reward estimation to improve embodied agents, including without ground-truth rewards.

paragraphs: Self-diffusion solves inverse problems by refining a candidate solution directly from observed data. Conventional diffusion approaches first learn a generative model from clean examples, then use it to produce solutions consistent with measurements. This framework instead starts with a randomly initialized convolutional network and needs no pretrained score model or external denoiser.

Its iterative process adds noise to the current estimate and trains the same self-denoising network for a number of iterations to predict a solution from that noisy input. Training uses a data-fidelity loss, which ties the prediction to the observations. Repeated noising and denoising exploit the neural network's spectral bias, with the noise schedule modulating how that bias shapes reconstruction.

The framework is designed to accommodate arbitrary forward operators and noisy observations. The reported experiments examine a variety of linear inverse problems, where it achieves competitive or superior performance against other methods. The findings show that useful diffusion-like refinement can emerge from training within the reconstruction process itself, without relying on a generative model learned beforehand from a clean dataset.
neurips-2025-self-diffusion-for-solving-.tldr: Self-diffusion reconstructs solutions through iterative noising and task-specific denoiser training, without a pretrained generative model.

paragraphs: SWE-RL uses the history of open-source software development as training material for reinforcement learning. That history includes code snapshots, changes, issues, and pull requests, providing examples of problems and their resolutions. The goal is to improve reasoning for real software engineering by learning from how projects evolve.

The method uses a lightweight rule-based reward, such as similarity between a generated solution and the recorded solution. This lets a model learn to recover developers' solutions and associated reasoning from software-evolution data. Applied to Llama 3, it produces Llama3-SWE-RL-70B, which solves 41.0% of SWE-bench Verified, a collection of human-verified GitHub issues. The authors report performance comparable to leading proprietary models such as GPT-4o.

Although reinforcement learning uses only software-evolution data, the resulting model also improves on five other task areas: function coding, library use, code reasoning, mathematics, and general language understanding. A supervised-fine-tuning baseline instead deteriorates on average. These results suggest that reinforcement learning on development histories can improve capabilities beyond the immediate software-repair training setting.
neurips-2025-swe-rl-advancing-llm-reason.tldr: SWE-RL trains on software-development histories to improve real-world issue solving and shows reasoning gains beyond its training domain.

paragraphs: This paper examines how Chatbot Arena's evaluation practices can distort model comparisons. It finds that some providers privately test multiple variants and selectively release results. Choosing the best score from several attempts creates selection bias: the public ranking reflects both measured performance and the opportunity to choose which measurements become visible.

The authors identify an extreme case involving 27 privately tested variants before one model appeared publicly in second place. They also find that proprietary models receive more battles and are removed less often than open alternatives, producing unequal access to Arena data. The two leading providers individually received an estimated 19.2% and 20.4% of the data, compared with 29.7% collectively for 83 open-weight models.

Under conservative estimates, the paper shows that additional Arena data can yield relative gains of up to 112% on ArenaHard, which comes from the Arena distribution. These findings connect selective disclosure and unequal data access to overfitting to the evaluation environment. The authors propose reforms aimed at making benchmarking fairer and more transparent while recognizing the platform's community contribution.
neurips-2025-the-leaderboard-illusion-0e.tldr: Selective private testing and unequal access to Arena data can bias leaderboard scores and encourage adaptation to the benchmark.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates a language model by having a smaller model draft several possible next tokens for parallel verification. Tree-based versions offer multiple candidates at each position. Existing verification often checks individual tokens from the root downward, discarding every descendant once a parent is rejected.

Traversal Verification reverses that direction, working from leaves toward the root and considering acceptance of the entire sequence along a path. This addresses two weaknesses identified by the authors: token probabilities do not capture sequence probabilities, and rejecting a parent can prematurely eliminate useful candidate subsequences. The new verification process preserves potentially valid subsequences that earlier schemes would discard, making better use of the drafted tree.

The authors prove that the resulting output distribution exactly matches the target model's distribution, providing a lossless inference guarantee. Experiments across multiple models and tasks show consistently longer accepted drafts and higher throughput than token-level verification. The contribution is therefore a change to the verification algorithm that improves speed while retaining the target model's sampling distribution.
neurips-2025-traversal-verification-for-.tldr: Traversal Verification checks speculative token sequences from leaves to root, improving throughput while provably preserving the target model's distribution.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can be tuned using human preferences, but feedback collected from different groups may be inconsistent. Diff-UAPA addresses that uncertainty as part of the policy-update process. Its goal is to align behavior with incoming preferences while reducing the disruptive influence of disagreements across user populations.

The algorithm uses an iterative framework in which the policy adapts incrementally to preferences from different groups. It optimizes a maximum-posterior objective that combines regret-based preferences with an informative Beta prior. The prior guides updates in the presence of uncertainty, while the objective enables direct optimization of the diffusion policy without requiring a specified reward function. This makes uncertainty handling part of the alignment procedure itself.

The authors evaluate Diff-UAPA on simulated and real-world robotics tasks under diverse human-preference configurations. Their experiments demonstrate robust and reliable alignment in these settings. The stated benefit is that a policy can incorporate successive groups' feedback while mitigating inconsistency, supporting preference learning where the people supplying judgments do not all share the same background.
neurips-2025-uncertainty-aware-preferenc.tldr: Diff-UAPA directly tunes diffusion policies to diverse human preferences using a Bayesian objective that mitigates inconsistent feedback.

paragraphs: Explicit reasoning can help solve difficult problems, yet this paper finds that it can also reduce compliance with instructions. The authors evaluate more than 20 models on IFEval, which uses simple verifiable constraints, and ComplexBench, which uses more complex combinations of constraints. They consistently observe performance drops when chain-of-thought prompting is applied.

Case studies distinguish situations where reasoning helps, such as formatting or lexical precision, from those where it hurts by overlooking simple constraints or adding unnecessary content. The authors introduce constraint attention, a measure of how much the model focuses on instruction-relevant tokens. Their attention analysis shows that chain-of-thought reasoning often shifts focus away from those tokens during generation.

They evaluate four mitigation strategies: in-context learning, self-reflection, self-selective reasoning, and classifier-selective reasoning. Selective approaches, particularly classifier-selective reasoning, substantially recover lost performance. The findings support choosing when to reason explicitly based on the task, rather than assuming that more visible reasoning consistently improves instruction following. They also separate success at complex reasoning from reliably respecting the requested output constraints.
neurips-2025-when-thinking-fails-the-pit.tldr: Chain-of-thought prompting can reduce instruction-following accuracy, while selectively enabling reasoning can recover much of the loss.

paragraphs: YOLOv12 redesigns a real-time object detector around attention mechanisms. Earlier YOLO architecture improvements largely centered on convolutional networks because attention-based models struggled to match their speed. The paper aims to combine attention's modeling benefits with the inference speed needed for real-time detection.

The reported results show improved accuracy with competitive latency across multiple model sizes. YOLOv12-N reaches 40.5% mean average precision with a 1.62-millisecond inference latency on a T4 GPU. At comparable speed, it exceeds YOLOv10-N and YOLO11-N by 2.0 and 1.1 percentage points of mAP, respectively. This comparison directly addresses the trade-off motivating the architecture: whether attention can improve detection without losing real-time speed.

The advantage also extends to comparisons with real-time detectors derived from DETR. YOLOv12-X outperforms RT-DETRv2-R101 and RT-DETRv3-R101 while running faster and using fewer computations and parameters. Together, these findings show that an attention-centered design can be competitive across accuracy, latency, and model resources in the reported comparisons, making attention a practical architectural option for the evaluated real-time detectors.
neurips-2025-yolov12-attention-centric-r.tldr: YOLOv12 makes attention central to real-time object detection, improving reported accuracy while maintaining competitive inference speed.

paragraphs: This paper builds efficient hybrid language models by transferring knowledge from existing pretrained Transformers. Its X-EcoMLA approach combines state space model layers with multi-head latent attention, using a refined initialization and post-training pipeline. The aim is to approach Transformer accuracy and state space model efficiency without repeating full pretraining.

The resulting family includes 1B, 3B, and 8B models trained using 7–11 billion tokens and an 8B teacher. Their key-value caches shrink to 3.9%, 2%, and 2.73% of the original sizes, respectively. On average zero-shot LM Harness performance, the smaller two variants preserve 100% of the original performance, while the 8B variant preserves more than 97%. These results pair large memory reductions with strong retention on the evaluated tasks.

The authors also report competitive or superior accuracy against comparison models while using fewer training tokens, smaller teachers, and less cache memory. The 8B variant exceeds Minitron-8B's few-shot accuracy by 7% and achieves 1.4–3.3 times MambaInLlama's throughput. The findings support hybrid conversion as an efficient way to reuse pretrained language-model knowledge.
neurips-2025-zebra-llama-towards-extreme.tldr: X-EcoMLA converts pretrained Transformer knowledge into hybrid models that sharply reduce cache memory while largely preserving evaluated accuracy.
